metadata.title: Claude, Expansion Update.
metadata.purpose: Answer one real question in the Teardown register: if we're expanding into a new state, can Claude just rewrite our handbook for it? Lands the carry-out that the skill runs one fixed checklist and flags sections, every time — but deciding what the new handbook actually says is still yours.

beats.narration_text: Someone asks: can Claude rewrite our handbook for the new state we're expanding into? Wrong first word. It doesn't produce a finished document — it compares the existing handbook against what the new state requires, and flags what needs work. Liam, take it from here.

beats.note: B00 is Remotion (BrutalistHesitantWriter) per hai-simple SKILL.md. Writer types the newcomer's wrong-guess word 'REWRITE' (implying Claude autonomously produces a finished, ready-to-publish handbook), hesitates, corrects to 'flag' -> lands 'Can Claude flag our handbook for the new state?'. The wrong guess is picked up directly by B03's stated scope (a comparison against a checklist, flagging sections, not a finished rewrite). Narration is ~46 words + lead_silence_s 0.8, giving the typing a >=9s window (TIMING LAW).

beats.narration_text: A skill is a folder Claude opens before it acts. This one is called expansion-update. Inside sits one file — SKILL.md — and the entire instruction set is there, in plain language a person can read. No hidden logic, no compiled binary underneath. They optimized for a reader over a compiler: the file you can read is the program that runs.

beats.narration_text: The pipeline lives in the Steps section of that file. Claude reads step one, runs it, moves to step two — top to bottom, no branching unless a step says to branch. They optimized for a predictable route over a clever one: same input, same path through, same output shape every run.

props.title: How the skill works.
props.sparkLine: Same input, same route, same output shape.

beats.narration_text: Here's what's actually happening. Take the existing handbook, walk it section by section against what the new state requires, and mark every section where the two don't line up. That's the whole job. They optimized for repeatable flagging over judgment — same checklist in, same flagged list out, every time. The flagged list is a queue for a human, not a set of edits.

props.heading: The interesting constraint.
props.body: Walk the handbook section by section; flag where the new state's rule doesn't match.
props.sparkLine: Same checklist in, same flagged list out.

beats.narration_text: Same checklist in, same flagged sections out, every time. The skill tells you which sections don't fit the new state yet. Deciding what to write in their place is still yours.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini: I'm on a legal team preparing to open an office in Colorado, and I'll paste our current employee handbook next. Play the role of a state-expansion checklist-runner: for Colorado's employer-specific rules — sick leave, meal and rest periods, final-paycheck timing, non-compete clauses, wage-transparency postings, and workers'-comp posting — flag every section of the handbook whose current language doesn't fit Colorado law. For each flagged section, give me the current language, the Colorado rule it collides with, and the exact question I should ask an employment lawyer before rewriting. Don't rewrite the language yourself — that decision is still mine. Go deeper: take the two most sensitive flagged sections and draft the exact intake questions I should send to our HR lead before we touch either, so we don't ship a change we didn't need to make.
